The Chamber of Deputies definitively approved the bill on antisemitism on Tuesday evening, 17 November, with 147 votes in favour, 93 against and 5 abstentions, writes Il Post. The Senate had already approved it in March; according to Euronews, the vote then was 105 in favour, 24 against and 21 abstentions. All opposition amendments were rejected. The text, promoted by the League's group leader in the Senate Massimiliano Romeo, adopts as a reference the definition of antisemitism by the IHRA, the intergovernmental alliance for Holocaust remembrance. Among the IHRA's examples are the denial of the Jewish people's right to self-determination and holding them collectively responsible for the actions of Israel.

Those who oppose it called for the 2021 «Jerusalem Declaration», which does not consider criticism of Israel based on evidence to be antisemitic. The US Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, said an investigation is under way into Alice Huang and her company, Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm. «There is an ongoing investigation into her company and her,» he said. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated in a television interview that the administration wants answers from Nvidia regarding chip sales to China: who was monitoring compliance with the rules and which levels of the company knew.

The affair is weighing on the markets. On Friday, Nvidia stock lost around 13% following news that the SEC, the US stock market regulator, is examining the company's accounting, according to two sources cited by the press. The slump in artificial intelligence-related stocks swept across Wall Street and Asian stock markets, where among the causes cited by analysts is precisely the scandal involving Nvidia, which has reopened calls for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced chips.

According to the Departments of Commerce and Justice, the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over possible export control violations. Alice Huang was questioned during an on-site inspection in June 2025; the criminal case was subsequently referred to the Department of Justice. An associate of Huang, Li Ming, is out on bail in Singapore: the city-state's charges relate to alleged false declarations to Super Micro Computer and do not name Megaspeed. Singapore police said they found insufficient evidence of offences linked to inaccurate statements by Huang, who received a stern warning for providing information believed to be knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role. Singapore has not investigated her for espionage.

According to a US press report, Alice Huang was allegedly in contact with an official from a major Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 to autumn 2026; there is no official confirmation. According to another account, the Department of Justice is verifying whether companies linked to Huang helped ship Super Micro products out of the US to China. Megaspeed says it is a «legitimate and compliant» company and that Huang left the firm in August 2025. Nvidia did not comment in the sources consulted.

The European Commission has proposed a new loan of up to €45 billion for Ukraine, intended for 2027. It is in addition to the €90 billion already approved for 2026 and 2027. The proposal is preliminary and must be approved by the European Parliament and the Council.

The proposal decides who finances Ukraine's defence and budget in 2027 and how long the common debt would remain the responsibility of the member states. The Ukrainian government says that with rising costs, another €70 billion is needed for 2027. The EU would cover two-thirds of that deficit, while allies such as the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada, Japan, and Australia would have to provide the remaining €25 billion.

Of the €45 billion, about €25 billion is for the purchase of weapons and about €20 billion for civilian expenses such as schools and hospitals. The loan would be financed with common debt: the Commission would issue bonds on behalf of all member states. Commission officials estimate interest of about €6 billion per year on the total loans, which member states would cover with subsidies so that they do not burden Ukraine.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Bulgaria have indicated that they will not participate, and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is opposed. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to veto the next EU budget if the 27 do not support the loan. The Commission is offering the four countries the option to join the €20 billion civilian portion and remain outside the €25 billion military portion.

Ukraine would only repay if Russia accepted war reparations in a future peace agreement; until then, the EU would renew the loan. The EU reserves the right to use frozen Russian assets, about €210 billion, for repayment.

For the first time, the Court has recognised a State as responsible for genocide. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed. Jurist Toby Cadman said that enforcement will depend on subsequent steps, such as intervention by the UN Security Council or sanctions.

The Court found that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of civilians, committed widespread sexual violence and also targeted those fleeing towards Bangladesh. The text cites evidence of approximately 10,000 Rohingya killed. The judges wrote that the only reasonable deduction from the atrocities is the intention to destroy a substantial part of the group. They added that Myanmar has failed to fulfil its obligation to prevent genocide.

The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019. Myanmar denies the accusation: it says that the 2017 offensive was a response to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army on police posts. The offensive pushed at least 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. According to the UN, over 1.3 million Rohingya are displaced in the region, 1.2 million of whom are in Cox's Bazar.

The work is coordinated by the South African organisation Barracuda Media, with over 200 journalists from more than 50 news outlets, including Italian ones, and is based on 15 million internal documents received from anonymous whistleblowers.

The German government is demanding accountability from the country's leading bank, and the documents touch upon Russian clients and the Jeffrey Epstein case. According to the investigation, for fifteen years the bank allegedly often ignored warnings about possible violations of anti-money laundering regulations, sanctions and internal rules in order to protect business and clients.

Among the cases are $580 million in suspicious transactions linked to Epstein and relationships with Russian clients, including oligarchs Oleg Deripaska and Viktor Vekselberg. There is also mention of 17 officials and oligarchs close to Putin already on a US Treasury list. Deficiencies in control systems reportedly emerged from the documents of the Italian branch. Chief Executive Officer Christian Sewing told the German newspaper Bild that these are «old matters» dating back up to twenty years and that the bank has «nothing to hide». He described the operation with Epstein as a «bank error». German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that the bank must explain «with absolute transparency» how it has remedied the deficiencies.

According to the reconstruction, the bank never made the internal investigation «Project Aetos» and its conclusions public. Deutsche Bank replies that the external auditor examined the results and concluded that no adjustments to previous financial statements were needed, and that all Italian operations are correctly reflected in the group's accounts.

According to Il Post, Eisenkot's bloc received 66 votes, including those of the two Arab-led parties. The speakership decides the timetable of parliamentary business; Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. Kahana said he will work in the interest of all, without distinctions of «religion, ethnicity or gender». Il Post writes that Eisenkot's grouping, which has already tabled bills to investigate Netanyahu, prevent his re-election and cancel certain reforms, intends to pass them before forming the government. The reactions of Netanyahu and Likud do not appear in the sources consulted.

Gadi Eisenkot says Netanyahu cannot remain prime minister while the alleged vote-rigging manoeuvres are under discussion, Al Jazeera reports. The Times of Israel writes that the police and the attorney-general are reportedly investigating to establish whether the prime minister's office orchestrated the scandal over the buying and selling of Arab votes: according to the report, Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ophir Zini, allegedly passed information from a former employee of the office to the police and requested wiretaps on five Arab MPs, a request rejected by the attorney-general. The prime minister's office speaks of «defamation» and Eisenkot has promised an inquiry. On 15 November the Yashar and Likud teams met without making progress, according to the Times of Israel, which adds that Netanyahu is reportedly open to excluding Ben Gvir and that parallel talks between Eisenkot's bloc and United Torah Judaism are reportedly making headway, which the party's leader denies.

On 14 November Benjamin Netanyahu again called for talks «without preconditions» for a national unity government, arguing that only a coalition of this type can guarantee Israel's security, Ansa, Al Jazeera and the Times of Israel report. Gadi Eisenkot rejected the proposal as «yet another trick», Ansa says, and recalled that meetings between the negotiating teams of Yashar and Likud are already scheduled for Sunday 15 November, according to Ansa and the Times of Israel. The Times of Israel also writes that Eisenkot is said to be prioritising a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties.

The bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot has decided to nominate Matan Kahana, of the Yashar party, for Knesset speaker, reports the Times of Israel, which also writes that the Knesset set up temporary committees after a heated debate. Again according to the Times of Israel, ultra-Orthodox leaders are receiving multiple coalition offers, and the rabbis of United Torah Judaism are demanding signed commitments from all 48 MPs of the Eisenkot bloc for a law on military service exemption. Eisenkot said Netanyahu was refusing to give him security briefings and requested the intervention of the attorney-general; later, the newspaper writes, he received the briefing, in which according to one account the military sees no urgent need to strike Iran.

On 10 November the 26th Knesset was sworn in and Benjamin Netanyahu, interim prime minister, called before the MPs for a national unity government, the Times of Israel reports. Gadi Eisenkot has the mandate to form the government, entrusted to him by President Herzog on Sunday 8 November, as Al Jazeera, Reuters and Il Post write. He has six weeks and needs 61 seats out of 120.

According to the Times of Israel, Netanyahu said that a narrow government cannot address security challenges. He argued that Ra'am and the Joint List want the destruction of the Jewish State, clarifying that he was not referring to Arab voters in general. He also warned the ultra-Orthodox parties against supporting an Eisenkot-led government, which he claimed would depend on the Arab parties. During the speech opposition MPs, including Bennett, interrupted him, recalling the alleged ties of his aides to Qatar and the refusal of a commission of inquiry into 7 October.

Eisenkot called the speech «full of hate» and said it confirms Netanyahu's unsuitability to remain in office, the Times of Israel writes. He reiterated his intention to form a «national emergency government». His party, Yashar, cancelled the meetings with Likud scheduled for Wednesday. The Joint List called the speech «delusional, inciting and racist», while the leader of Ra'am, Mansour Abbas, said Netanyahu used a state occasion to incite against Arab parties and that Ra'am supports two states and condemns terrorism.

The figures are those of the 27 October vote: 48 seats for Eisenkot's alliance, 53 for Netanyahu's bloc and a record 19 for the Arab-led parties, Al Jazeera writes. In the consultations, 67 seats endorsed Eisenkot and 46 Netanyahu, Al Jazeera, the Times of Israel and Reuters report. According to Reuters, the 67 include the 19 of the two Arab-led parties, which Eisenkot does not want in government for now. Al Jazeera reports that he says he is open to a government with Netanyahu and Smotrich if Likud and Religious Zionism support him. According to the Times of Israel, three Jewish opposition parties have so far refused to ally with Arab parties, and it is unclear whether United Torah Judaism will enter the government: it rejects compulsory national service for all, a principle of Eisenkot's.

The Department of the Army says it wants to proceed «to have optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures in place». The UN climate summit, COP31, closed on Sunday 22 November in Antalya, Turkey, without a final agreement, after a prolonged extension. The text presented by the co-presidencies of Turkey and Australia was rejected by the European Union and other countries because it made no mention of fossil fuels. According to sources' reconstructions, it is the first failure of an annual climate conference since the Copenhagen summit in 2009.

The draft would have recognised for the first time in an official text that global warming is on a trajectory exceeding 1.5 degrees. In the revised version, the target of 120 billion dollars to help poor countries adapt had been removed. Delegates from various countries described the text as too weak to address warming.

The European Union said it would not approve an agreement «that does not even mention fossil fuels». Denmark's Climate Minister, Samira Nawa, explained that the EU would have accepted the clauses on adaptation funds, but that strong commitments on emission reductions and reference to science were lacking. For British negotiator Kate Hughes, the draft «takes us backwards from the science».

The front opposed to the word «fossils» includes oil- and gas-producing countries. The Saudi Arabian delegation said that «climate change requires all solutions on the table» and that «concrete solutions» must not be taken away. The Russian delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, said Russia «cannot accept any wording on fossil fuels», warning that less oil and gas supply could lead to energy poverty. Iraq expressed «deep concern» over passages it said move away from the Paris Agreement.

Island and most vulnerable nations spoke of betrayal. The Marshall Islands say they were «disappointed by all sides», Vanuatu called the silence on fossils unacceptable, and the group of least developed countries, 44 nations with over a billion inhabitants, said it could not accept steps backwards. Kenya complained that the text did not respond to Africa's needs.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was «deeply disappointed». Chris Bowen, Australia's Climate Minister and chair of the negotiations, said that «an obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels» and that some parties would veto any text mentioning it. Murat Kurum, the Turkish Environment Minister and president of COP31, said there will be no new text and that work will focus on implementing decisions already taken.
